newsitem.title: USA: Republicans set game plan to defend welfare law.
newsitem.headline: Republicans set game plan to defend welfare law.

text.p: House Republicans crafted a detailed strategy for selling the new welfare law to voters, including "Oprah-style" town meetings where former recipients share success stories, a copy of the plan showed Wednesday.

The "member's guide to explaining the new welfare law" also suggested lawmakers hold press events with handicapped children who did not lose benefits under the law, which ended disability aid to 135,000 children with behavioural disorders.

Appearing with a child who still receives Supplemental Security Income (SSI) illustrates that children with severe ailments will continue to get the help they need, according to a copy of the guide obtained by Reuters.

Republicans said they were forced to overhaul the SSI programme because children were being coached to feign behavioural problems to qualify for benefits. The Social Security Administration did not find widespread abuse.

"Show your side of the story before your opponents strike first," the guide said. It warned that "disability advocates have stepped up their campaign to convince the nation that any reform of the SSI children's programme is unfair and will gravely harm needy children."

Marty Ford of The Arc, which represents the mentally retarded, said the strategy "seems so cynical. Holding a news conference with children who didn't get kicked off begs the question. Who are the children who did get kicked off?"
Florida Republican Representative Clay Shaw, who crafted the guide, said lawmakers simply needed good information to respond to growing public questions as the law took effect.
"There is going to be a lot of interest out there. They (lawmakers) are getting more and more stories of people who might fall through the cracks," Shaw said.

He denied there was anything defensive about the document, calling it a "question of staying on the offence." Republicans also formed a nine-member communications group to coordinate information on welfare.

The 17-page guide, sent to all House Republicans earlier this month, recommends lawmakers try to locate someone in their district who had received Food Stamps, but now works year-round due to tough new work rules in the measure.

Under the law, able-bodied people without dependents can receive Food Stamps for no more than three months in any three-year period, unless they work part time. Forty state governors have sought exemptions from the requirement.
Other tips include hiring welfare enrollees to work in lawmakers' offices and setting up job fairs with a local Chamber of Commerce or business group.

Lawmakers were encouraged to visit drug rehabilitation centres and speak with people who were receiving SSI, but are now in recovery. Congress ended SSI benefits to drug addicts and alcoholics, diverting some of savings to treatment.
The guide laid out important dates for implementing the welfare law and provides facts on its myriad provisions.

It encouraged Republicans to highlight recent statistics showing average welfare caseloads have fallen 16 percent from a historic high of 1994-1995 to September, 1996. Declining caseloads mean states have more money than expected to implement new work requirements in the law.

The welfare law gave states broad power to design their own welfare programmes. Aid was limited to five years and work required after two. Most of the savings in the law came from ending aid to legal immigrants and cutting Food Stamps.
